Alabama enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament at 23-9 overall and 13-5 in SEC play, good for second place in the league and a No. 4 seed in the Midwest Region, with a first-round game scheduled for March 20, 2026 against No. 13 seed Hofstra. Their most recent game before the field was set was an 80-79 SEC Tournament loss to Ole Miss on March 13, after they closed the regular season by beating Auburn 96-84 on March 7 to finish 23-8 and 13-5 in conference play. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/team/schedule/_/id/333/season/2026))

From a traditional scouting perspective, Alabama under Nate Oats is still built around pace, paint attacks, and volume threes, but this year’s version is more guard-driven than some of his earlier teams. The clearest statistical markers are that Alabama averaged 92.1 points per game through its first 19 games, hit 233 threes in those 19 games, and by the Ole Miss game notes on February 9 was making 12.6 threes per game, which ranked No. 1 in the SEC and No. 2 nationally. That profile shows up in actual game examples: Alabama scored 115 against UNLV on November 25, 105 against Maryland on November 26, 102 against Yale on December 29, and 100 against both Texas A&M on February 4 and Mississippi State on February 25. In the February 25 win over Mississippi State, Alabama made 22 threes, and in the first half alone made 16, which Alabama Athletics identified as the most made threes in a half under Oats. ([rolltide.com](https://rolltide.com/documents/download/2026/1/26/Game20_MIssouri.pdf))

Specific personnel usage tells you the scheme. Labaron Philon Jr. is the primary creator, leading Alabama in scoring at 21.4 points per game and assists at 4.9 per game. Aden Holloway gives them a second ballhandler and spacer at 16.9 points and 4.1 assists per game. Amari Allen supplies frontcourt rebounding and slashing at 7.5 rebounds per game, while Aiden Sherrell is the rim-running big and shot blocker at 2.4 blocks per game. When Alabama is humming, it is usually Philon or Holloway turning a high ball screen into a paint touch, then spraying to shooters like Latrell Wrightsell Jr. or lifting the ball to Sherrell. The concrete game evidence is strong: Holloway had 10 assists in the 100-75 win over Mississippi State on February 25; Philon had 7 assists in the 117-115 double-overtime win over Arkansas on February 18; Alabama’s road win at Ole Miss on February 11 featured a 13-2 opening run to the second half fueled by three made threes; and Wrightsell hit seven threes for 21 points in the 90-64 win over Missouri on January 27. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/team/stats/_/id/0333/sort/freeThrowsMade?utm_source=openai))

The half-court menu is not exotic, but it is specific: spread high pick-and-roll for Philon, slot ball screens for Holloway, five-out or four-out spacing to create driving gaps, and drag-screen actions in early offense before the defense is set. Alabama also uses trail threes and secondary break actions aggressively; the evidence is the shot volume and score jumps after rebounds or live-ball changes. Against Auburn on March 7, Alabama turned a 15-5 run in 2:29 early in the second half into a 67-39 lead. Against Ole Miss on February 11, they came out of halftime with three quick threes during a 13-2 run. Against Texas A&M on February 4, they scored 100 despite a one-possession final margin, showing they are comfortable playing games in the 90s or higher. ([rolltide.com](https://rolltide.com/news/2026/3/7/mens-basketball-no-16-16-alabama-defeats-auburn-96-84-to-sweep-season-series))

Defensively, the philosophy is more disruption than containment. Alabama wants turnovers, blocked shots, and transition chances more than it wants a low-possession grind. The March 7 Auburn recap quoted Oats saying forcing turnovers had been “an emphasis” lately, and Alabama had forced 13-plus turnovers in back-to-back games at that point and double-digit turnovers in four of its last five. Sherrell anchors the back line; he posted 8 blocks against Clemson on December 3 and 8 more against Arizona on December 13, while Alabama’s team high for blocked shots in an SEC statistical packet was 15 against Arizona. That said, the risk in Alabama’s pressure-and-rotate style is obvious in its losses. Florida scored 100 on Alabama on February 1, Tennessee won 79-73 in Tuscaloosa on January 24 after scoring 43 in the second half, and Georgia hung 98 on them on March 3. Earlier in the year, Alabama allowed 96 to St. John’s in a win, 95 to Gonzaga in a loss, 96 to Arizona in a loss, and 93 to South Florida in a win. This is a defense built to create swings, not one that guarantees control every trip. ([rolltide.com](https://rolltide.com/news/2026/3/7/mens-basketball-no-16-16-alabama-defeats-auburn-96-84-to-sweep-season-series?utm_source=openai))

Oats’ coaching philosophy remains analytically aggressive, but this team has shown a documented ability to adjust game to game and half to half. After dropping three of four SEC games from January 7 through February 1, Alabama responded with a major correction. On January 27, after a 79-73 home loss to Tennessee and a 100-77 blowout loss at Florida, Alabama hammered Missouri 90-64. On February 11 at Ole Miss, Alabama scored only 32 first-half points and shot 25 percent before erupting for 61 in the second half. On February 18 against Arkansas, Alabama came back from a 14-point deficit and shot 76 percent from the field in the second half to win in double overtime. On March 7 against Auburn, Alabama answered a Tiger comeback with an 8-2 run to push the margin back over 20. Those are concrete examples of Oats teams changing coverage intensity, increasing tempo, and re-centering the offense around downhill guard play after halftime. ([rolltide.com](https://rolltide.com/news/2026/1/27/mens-basketball-strong-second-half-performance-helps-no-23-23-alabama-down-missouri-90-64?utm_source=openai))

Clutch execution is one of the most important parts of this report because Alabama has lived in close games. The positive examples: they beat Oklahoma 83-81 on January 17; beat Texas A&M 100-97 on February 4; beat Auburn 96-92 on February 7 at Neville Arena; won a double-overtime game over Arkansas 117-115 on February 18; beat LSU 90-83 on February 21; and won at Tennessee 71-69 on February 28. The Tennessee road win is especially relevant for tournament scouting because it was a lower-possession game outside Alabama’s preferred scoring range, and Wrightsell’s 25 points carried the offense. The concern is that they have also dropped close late-game spots: 92-88 to Texas on January 10 after erasing a 13-point second-half deficit but failing in the final minutes, 98-88 at Georgia on March 3, and 80-79 to Ole Miss in the SEC Tournament on March 13. So the late-game profile is not soft; it is volatile. Alabama can finish, but it is not immune to execution lapses when the game gets into the final two possessions. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/team/schedule/_/id/333/season/2026))

The key players start with Philon. He is Alabama’s engine, averaging 21.4 points and 4.9 assists, and his biggest recent moments include 35 points and 7 assists against Arkansas on February 18, 32 points at Mississippi State on January 13, 26 points against Tennessee on January 24, 25 points at Auburn on February 7, and 28 points in the SEC Tournament loss to Ole Miss on March 13. Oats’ offense trusts him with the ball late, and he also passed 1,000 career points on March 7 against Auburn, becoming the fourth-fastest player in Alabama history to reach that mark at 66 games. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/team/stats/_/id/0333/sort/freeThrowsMade?utm_source=openai))

Holloway is the second guard defenses must game-plan for. He averages 16.9 points and 4.1 assists, had 26 against Yale on December 29, 26 against Kentucky on January 3, 20 against Texas A&M on February 4, 20 against South Carolina on February 14, and shared the March 7 Auburn lead with 21. His value is that he can punish teams that load up on Philon and can also play on or off the ball. ([sports-reference.com](https://www.sports-reference.com/cbb/schools/alabama/men/2026.html?utm_source=openai))

Allen is the glue forward. ESPN lists him as Alabama’s rebounding leader at 7.5 per game, and his game log includes 25 points and 11 rebounds at Vanderbilt on January 7, 23 points in the 100-75 win over Mississippi State on February 25, 19 against Arkansas on February 18, and 16 against Auburn on March 7. He is the player who stabilizes lineups when Alabama goes smaller or more perimeter-oriented. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/team/stats/_/id/0333/sort/freeThrowsMade?utm_source=openai))

Sherrell is the most important interior piece. He averages 2.4 blocks per game, had 8 blocks against Clemson and Arizona, posted 26 points and 13 rebounds against Arkansas on February 18, and had double-doubles or near-double-doubles in multiple February wins, including 12 points and 10 rebounds at LSU on February 21. He is the main reason Alabama can survive aggressive perimeter pressure without giving up a layup line every possession. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/team/stats/_/id/0333/sort/freeThrowsMade?utm_source=openai))

Wrightsell is the swing shooter. He exploded for 21 points on seven threes against Missouri on January 27, 21 more at Ole Miss on February 11, and 25 at Tennessee on February 28. Alabama named him SEC Player of the Week entering the final week. When Wrightsell stretches the floor, Alabama’s offense becomes much harder to load against because Philon and Holloway see cleaner driving lanes. ([rolltide.com](https://rolltide.com/news/2026/1/27/mens-basketball-strong-second-half-performance-helps-no-23-23-alabama-down-missouri-90-64?utm_source=openai))

The notable wins are strong and revealing. Alabama beat No. 5 St. John’s 103-96 on the road on November 8, showing it could win a high-end pace game away from home. It beat Kentucky 89-74 on January 3, a 15-point opening SEC statement. It won at Auburn 96-92 on February 7 and then beat Auburn again 96-84 on March 7, proving it could handle rivalry pressure in both venues. The February 18 117-115 double-overtime win over No. 20 Arkansas showed real resilience after a 14-point hole. The February 28 71-69 win at No. 22 Tennessee showed Alabama could also survive a half-court, possession-by-possession game. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/team/schedule/_/id/333/season/2026))

The losses also matter because they map the blueprint to beat Alabama. Purdue beat them 87-80 on November 13, Gonzaga beat them 95-85 on November 24, and Arizona beat them 96-75 on December 13, all suggesting elite offenses can score through Alabama’s pressure. Texas won 92-88 in Tuscaloosa on January 10 by staying poised late. Florida’s 100-77 win on February 1 was the most alarming defensive collapse, and Georgia’s 98-88 win on March 3 showed Alabama can still be dragged into a game it does not fully control if the opponent scores efficiently and keeps pace. The SEC Tournament loss to Ole Miss, 80-79 on March 13, is the freshest warning sign: Alabama entered March with an eight-game SEC winning streak, but still got knocked out immediately in Nashville. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/team/schedule/_/id/333/season/2026))

As for Oats’ NCAA Tournament history, Alabama Athletics lists five NCAA appearances under him from 2021 through 2025. Alabama reached the Sweet 16 in 2021, the Sweet 16 again in 2023, the Final Four in 2024, and the Sweet 16 in 2025. Alabama Athletics also noted after the 2024 Final Four loss to UConn that Oats was 8-4 in NCAA Tournament games at Alabama at that point, and a March 2025 Alabama release documented that the Tide advanced to a third straight Sweet 16 with an 80-66 win over Saint Mary’s. In short, Oats has built a program that is no longer merely dangerous; it now has repeated second-weekend proof. ([rolltide.com](https://rolltide.com/sports/2026/2/27/ncaa-tournament-history?utm_source=openai))

Bottom line: Alabama is a high-ceiling, high-variance tournament team. The strengths are obvious and backed by game evidence: elite guard creation from Philon and Holloway, explosive spacing when Wrightsell gets loose, shot-blocking from Sherrell, and multiple proven wins over NCAA-level opponents including Auburn twice, Tennessee on the road, Arkansas, Kentucky, and St. John’s. The vulnerabilities are just as concrete: they have allowed 100 to Florida, 98 to Georgia, 96 to Arizona, 95 to Gonzaga, and 92 to Texas. If Alabama controls pace and gets downhill from its guards, it can make the second weekend. If an opponent forces it into a turnover-neutral, defensively disciplined game while still scoring efficiently, the Tide is vulnerable to another one-possession or late-possession exit. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/team/schedule/_/id/333/season/2026))

Alabama enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament profile as one of the clearest high-variance contenders in the field: elite offense, extreme tempo, a résumé validated by brutal schedule strength, and a defense that drifts far enough backward to create real second-weekend volatility. On the tournament team sheet, Alabama sits at NET No. 17 with a 23-8 Division I record, including 7-7 in Quadrant 1 and 9-1 in Quadrant 2. WarrenNolan’s team sheet also lists Alabama at No. 14 in ESPN BPI, No. 15 in KenPom/POM, and No. 16 in T-Rank, with NET strength of schedule No. 1 nationally and non-conference NET SOS No. 5. Result-based metrics are even more bullish: KPI No. 8, SOR No. 9, and WAB No. 9. Those numbers paint Alabama as a team whose body of work is fully tournament-worthy even if the predictive systems stop short of true top-10 status. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/team-net-sheet?team=Alabama&utm_source=openai))

The core statistical identity is straightforward. Alabama is one of the country’s best offenses by possession. WarrenNolan lists the Crimson Tide with an offensive rating of 122.6 points per 100 possessions, which ranks 13th nationally. But that offensive quality is paired with a defensive rating of 110.0, only 227th nationally. The resulting net rating is +11.6, good but not dominant relative to a true national-title favorite. That split is the whole Alabama story: the offense is absolutely tournament-caliber; the defense is much more fragile than the team’s reputation, talent level, or highlight package might suggest. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/stats-adv-offensive-rating?utm_source=openai))

Their pace amplifies everything. Sports-Reference’s season snapshot had Alabama at 91.8 points per game, 3rd nationally, while also allowing 82.7 points per game, 353rd of 365 teams, through the mid-February portion of the season. That is not just “fast”; it is structurally inflationary. Alabama’s raw scoring environment makes them look overwhelming offensively and messy defensively at the same time. The advanced numbers confirm that both impressions are partly true. Even once adjusted, the offense remains top-15 level, while the defense still grades as a genuine weakness. In practical tournament terms, Alabama can bury teams in a 6-minute avalanche, but it is also easier than usual for opponents to stay alive because the game contains more possessions and more shot volume. ([sports-reference.com](https://www.sports-reference.com/cbb/schools/alabama/men/2026-gamelogs-advanced.html?utm_source=openai))

On the shot-profile side, Alabama looks very much like a Nate Oats team. WarrenNolan lists the Tide with a 55.6% effective field goal rate and a 32.3% offensive rebounding rate. NCAA team stats show Alabama averaging 12.8 made threes per game, second nationally at the time of the update. Sports-Reference’s advanced game log page also showed the team averaging a 3-point attempt rate of .466 in its opening game and reflected the general shape of the season: Alabama consistently plays with high pace and heavy perimeter volume. Even where an exact season-long 3PA rate is not directly accessible, the available evidence strongly indicates an attack built around early-clock threes, spacing, and pressure through volume rather than through foul-drawing alone. This is not a grind-and-post offense; it is a possession-maximizing, shot-distribution offense. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/stats-adv-efg-percent?utm_source=openai))

Ball security appears better than the stereotype of a turbo-paced team might imply. Alabama’s own game notes listed the Tide at 9.8 turnovers per game as of early February, with a 1.5 assist/turnover ratio. That matters because high-possession teams can sometimes look sloppier than they really are; Alabama pushes pace without hemorrhaging empty trips. I cannot verify an exact season-long offensive turnover percentage from a public primary source in the search results, but the available turnover-per-game evidence suggests the Tide are at least solid, and likely better than average, at protecting possessions relative to style. That complements the eFG and offensive rebounding numbers: they create efficient shots, get extra possessions, and do not give away too many possessions themselves. ([rolltide.com](https://rolltide.com/documents/download/2026/2/9/Game24_OleMiss.pdf?utm_source=openai))

Free-throw pressure is harder to pin down precisely from the accessible public endpoints. Sports-Reference’s game log shows game-level FTr data, and WarrenNolan tracks free-throw attempt rate as a category, but the search results did not expose Alabama’s exact season-long rank/value in the snippet. So the best synthesis is this: Alabama’s offense is not primarily carried by free throws; the stronger statistical signatures are eFG, three-point volume, pace, and offensive rebounding. In other words, the Tide’s offense is more explosive than bruising. That can be a positive in tournament settings when games become shot-making contests, but it also makes them more variance-sensitive than teams that can manufacture offense at the line when perimeter rhythm disappears. ([sports-reference.com](https://www.sports-reference.com/cbb/schools/alabama/men/2026-gamelogs-advanced.html?utm_source=openai))

The résumé quality is excellent. Alabama’s NET sheet shows wins over Illinois, Saint John’s, Tennessee, Auburn twice, Arkansas, Kentucky, Clemson, and Texas A&M, plus strong road wins at Tennessee, Auburn, Oklahoma, LSU, and Ole Miss. The flip side is that the losses are mostly to very good teams as well: Arizona, Florida, Gonzaga, Purdue, Vanderbilt, Georgia, Texas, and Tennessee. That profile is exactly what you expect from a high-end SEC team that challenged itself aggressively. With NET SOS No. 1 and RPI SOS No. 4, Alabama has essentially no résumé fraud in its file. If predictive metrics are a little cooler than résumé metrics, the explanation is not schedule padding; it is the defense. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/team-net-sheet?team=Alabama&utm_source=openai))

Recent form is positive enough to matter. Alabama’s late results on the team sheet show road wins at Tennessee on February 28, at Georgia on March 3, and a home win over Auburn on March 7. That closing stretch, especially the two rivalry/road data points, suggests the team was not limping into March. Without a directly accessible public top-line “last 10 games efficiency trend” value from Torvik, the best evidence-based synthesis is that Alabama’s form improved at the end through better result quality more than through a fundamental change in identity. They still looked like Alabama: huge scoring totals, lots of possessions, narrow margins even in wins, and enough offensive firepower to beat top competition anywhere. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/team-net-sheet?team=Alabama&utm_source=openai))

This is where the numbers diverge from the eye test. The eye test often says Alabama is overwhelming, because 90-point outputs, transition bursts, and three-point barrages are vivid. The numbers say something more nuanced: Alabama is absolutely dangerous enough to beat almost anyone, but the defense is weak enough that they are not as stable as a typical top-15 predictive team. A casual viewer might think “final four upside,” and that is true. The metrics add the warning label: “also vulnerable to a hot opponent in a one-game sample.” In fact, the most conventional wisdom-defying number in the profile may be the defensive one. A team with Alabama’s ceiling, talent, and schedule profile sitting 227th in defensive rating is not normal for a protected seed. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/stats-adv-defensive-rating?utm_source=openai))

Bottom line: Alabama’s 2026 tournament profile is driven by a top-15 offense, massive game tempo, elite schedule strength, and a résumé that compares favorably with many higher-seeded teams. The Crimson Tide are credible contenders because 122.6 points per 100 possessions, elite three-point volume, strong offensive rebounding, and decent ball security can carry a team through multiple rounds. But the 110.0 defensive rating, middling predictive placement relative to résumé ranking, and inflated-possession environment make them one of the bracket’s more dangerous-yet-fragile teams. If the threes fall, Alabama can look unstoppable. If the opponent survives the first punch, the underlying numbers say this team is more beatable than the brand name suggests. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/stats-adv-offensive-rating?utm_source=openai))
matchup-analyst:
Alabama enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament as an Oats team in its clearest form: extreme tempo, heavy 3-point volume, aggressive rim pressure, and lineups built to play fast around lead guard Labaron Philon Jr. Alabama was averaging 92.1 points per game in early March, a figure CBS cited as No. 1 nationally before the March 3 game at Georgia. The game logs also show the style: Alabama scored 103 at St. John’s on November 8, 115 vs. UNLV on November 25, 105 vs. Maryland on November 26, 104 vs. South Florida on December 17, and 102 vs. Yale on December 29. They attempted 57 threes vs. UTSA and 54 vs. Yale, which tells you the shot diet is still built around early-clock threes and drive-kick volume. ([cbssports.com](https://www.cbssports.com/college-basketball/gametracker/recap/NCAAB_20260303_BAMA%40UGA?utm_source=openai))

The specific way to disrupt that style is to take away clean first-side threes, force Alabama to finish possessions through contact in traffic, and dominate the glass after the initial contest. Tennessee gave the clearest blueprint on January 24, when Alabama lost 79-73 despite leading 39-36 at halftime. In that game, Alabama made a season-low six threes, Tennessee won the rebounding battle 42-33, and the Vols destroyed Alabama on the glass 27-16 in the second half. That matters because Alabama usually survives mediocre defensive possessions by winning the math battle with 3s; Tennessee cut off that escape hatch. Arizona used a different version of the same formula on December 13: after halftime it outscored Alabama 33-11 in the first 10:36, outrebounded the Tide 28-13 in the second half with an 11-1 offensive-rebound edge, and turned nine Alabama second-half turnovers into a 15-2 points-off-turnovers margin. ([rolltide.com](https://rolltide.com/news/2026/1/24/mens-basketball-no-17-17-alabama-drops-79-73-contest-to-tennessee?utm_source=openai))

On press and ball-pressure vulnerability: Alabama is not a classic turnover-prone chaos offense, but physical perimeter teams can knock it off rhythm. Alabama’s own January 25 notes showed it was just 6-3 when it had more turnovers than the opponent, versus 7-2 when it had fewer. Tennessee’s five-game run of success against Alabama was described by Tennessee media as beginning with “an abundance of turnovers,” and even though Alabama improved its ball security in later meetings, Tennessee still kept the offense from reaching normal efficiency. Arizona again is the best recent example of pressure turning into collapse: nine second-half turnovers and only 4-for-15 shooting early in the half as the Wildcats flipped the game. That suggests the tactical answer is not token full-court pressure; it is hard, connected point-of-attack pressure that blows up Alabama’s first action and forces Philon or Aden Holloway to initiate later in the clock. ([rolltide.com](https://rolltide.com/documents/download/2026/1/26/Game20_MIssouri.pdf))

On zone vulnerability, the hard truth is the public 2026 evidence is thinner than the man-pressure evidence. Alabama’s shot profile usually punishes passive zone because Oats’ spacing creates high-volume catch-and-shoot 3s; for example, Alabama hit 12 threes against Clemson and 22 against Yale. But there is a useful qualifier: Alabama is more vulnerable to matchup zones or changing zones after dead balls than to static 2-3 coverage. Clemson’s comeback on December 3 came after Alabama built a 19-point lead, then got outscored 24-9 over the first 8:04 of the second half before recovering late. The lesson is that changing the picture can slow Alabama, but only if the zone also finishes the possession with a rebound. If you zone and fail to rebound, Alabama’s size-athleticism front line will hurt you on second shots. ([rolltide.com](https://rolltide.com/news/2025/12/3/mens-basketball-no-12-12-alabama-defeats-clemson-90-84-in-acc-sec-challenge))

Preferred pace is obvious: Alabama wants the game played in the 80s or 90s. RealGM game splits list Alabama possessions in the mid-70s to mid-80s in several marquee games: 85.5 vs. St. John’s, 79.5 vs. UTSA, 75.4 vs. Maryland, and 69.9 vs. Purdue. When Alabama gets dragged into a more half-court, bruising script, the offense becomes more human. Tennessee held Alabama to 73; Arizona limited Alabama to 34 second-half points; Georgia beat Alabama 98-88 by winning the shotmaking battle without letting Alabama create the usual turnover/second-chance gap; then Alabama’s response against Auburn showed the counterexample, as Alabama controlled for 39:12, forced 13-plus turnovers for the second straight game, and grabbed 19 offensive rebounds in a 96-84 win. To force the opposite pace, you must make Alabama defend long possessions, send two back on the shot to kill runouts, and use the full clock after scores. Do not take quick, bad transition 3s against them; that just feeds their preferred game. ([basketball.realgm.com](https://basketball.realgm.com/ncaa/conferences/Southeastern-Conference/8/Alabama/253/stats/2026/Advanced_Stats/Qualified/Sr/December/All/per/asc/1/))

Position by position, Alabama’s matchup issues are specific. At point guard, the engine is Labaron Philon Jr. (6-4), who on the official roster is bigger than many college lead guards and strong enough to get downhill. He had 29 against Clemson, 24 and 10 rebounds against Arizona, 26 against Tennessee, 35 against Arkansas, and 21 against Auburn. If your 1 is undersized, Philon is a problem in the lane and on switches. At the other guard spot, Aden Holloway is only 6-1, so bigger guards can shoot over him or force switches onto him; Tennessee’s Nate Ament and Ja’Kobi Gillespie combined for 53 in the January 24 win, and Arkansas guard Darius Acuff Jr. exploded for 49 in the February 18 double-OT game that Oats admitted Alabama defended poorly. On the wings, Jalil Bethea (6-5), Amari Allen, London Jemison, Houston Mallette (6-5), and Taylor Bol Bowen give Alabama length and lineup flexibility, but Clemson showed a strong forward like RJ Godfrey could still score 19 efficiently and Clemson produced 50 paint points. Up front, Aiden Sherrell is the key tournament swing piece: 6-11, 255, real shot-blocking pop, 26 points and 13 rebounds vs. Arkansas, 10 rebounds and eight blocks vs. Clemson, eight blocks vs. Arizona, and multiple 20-plus point games per the game notes. But he can be pulled into space and made to defend repeated screening actions; Alabama’s rim protection is best when Sherrell can stay near the basket. ([rolltide.com](https://rolltide.com/sports/mens-basketball/roster))

Isolation vs. team offense tendency: Alabama is still much more of a team offense than an iso offense, but the exact 2026 Synergy split percentages were not accessible from publicly fetchable primary pages during this search. The usable on-record evidence points the same way. In Alabama’s best offensive games, the assist totals spike: 29 assists vs. Maryland, 22 vs. Yale, 22 vs. UTSA, and 22 vs. North Dakota. Philon is the late-clock bailout option, yet the structure is still drive-kick-swing rather than stationary mismatch hunting. When the ball sticks, Alabama becomes easier to guard; Arizona held Alabama to 1-for-9 from deep by the 7:36 mark of the second half, while Tennessee forced Alabama into just six made threes for the game. So the practical read is: make Philon and Holloway play east-west and late-clock, because Alabama is at its best when the first drive triggers the second and third pass. ([rolltide.com](https://rolltide.com/documents/download/2026/1/26/Game20_MIssouri.pdf))

Transition offense and defense are central. Official shot charts show Alabama scored 10 fast-break points against Gonzaga and 7 against Clemson, while allowing 16 fast-break points to Gonzaga and 12 to Clemson. Oats himself said after Clemson that Alabama gave up transition layups on the first two possessions of the second half and turned a comfortable margin into a dogfight. That is the opening: Alabama wants to run, but it can also be scored on before its half-court defense sets, especially if its guards are below the ball after missed 3s. Conversely, you must be disciplined getting back because their own transition attack is one of the nation’s most explosive. ([rolltide.com](https://rolltide.com/documents/download/2025/11/25/Game5_Gonzaga_2526.PDF))

Coaching adaptability is real. Oats does make game-to-game and in-game changes, but the staff is still philosophically aggressive rather than conservative. The strongest recent evidence is Alabama’s bounce-back from the March 3 Georgia loss to the March 7 Auburn win. Oats explicitly referenced that Alabama had been crushed by Georgia in points off turnovers and second-chance/extra-possession areas, then four days later Alabama flipped those exact categories against Auburn, forcing turnovers and grabbing 19 offensive rebounds. In-game, Alabama also closed Clemson on an 8-1 run over the final 2:40 after Clemson had taken an 83-81 lead. That suggests the staff can fix specific problem areas quickly, but it does not always prevent midgame defensive lulls; Clemson and Arizona both produced massive second-half surges. Concrete gameplan: To beat Alabama you must do five things. First, cut off the first-side 3 by top-locking shooters and shrinking gaps early; Tennessee held them to a season-low six made 3s.
